what_its_for: Belimumab is used to treat adults and some children (5 years and older) with lupus (also called systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE). It helps control your immune system, which in lupus attacks your own body by mistake. It can also treat a type of lupus that affects your kidneys, called lupus nephritis. This medicine does not cure lupus, but it can help reduce flares (times when symptoms get worse) and may let you take less of other lupus medicines over time.
how_to_take: Belimumab comes in two forms: (1) An IV infusion given through a needle in your vein at a doctor's office or clinic. Each infusion takes about 1 hour. (2) A shot (injection) that you or a caregiver can give under the skin (subcutaneous injection) at home, once you have been trained by your healthcare team. Common injection sites are the belly area or thigh. Rotate injection sites each time. Do not inject into skin that is bruised, red, tender, or hard. If you receive the IV form, a nurse or doctor will give it to you, so you do not need to prepare it yourself.
dosing: IV infusion: The usual adult dose is 10 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given on day 0, then again at 2 weeks, then at 4 weeks, and then every 4 weeks after that. For children (5 years and older), the dose is also weight-based and is decided by your doctor. Subcutaneous injection: The usual adult dose is 200 mg injected under the skin once every week. Your doctor will decide the best form and dose for you based on your specific condition. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: IV infusion: If you miss your scheduled infusion appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not wait until your next scheduled appointment. Subcutaneous injection: If you miss your weekly shot, give it as soon as you remember — unless your next scheduled dose is less than 2 days away. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular weekly schedule. Do not give two shots at the same time to make up for a missed dose. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Subcutaneous autoinjector or prefilled syringe: Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep in the original carton to protect from light. You may take it out of the refrigerator and let it sit at room temperature for up to 12 hours before injecting, but do not use it after 12 hours at room temperature if you plan to put it back in the fridge. Do not shake the autoinjector or syringe. IV infusion: The hospital or clinic will handle storage and preparation of the IV form. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children. Do not use if the medicine looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles in it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine, yellow fever vaccine, or shingles vaccine Zostavax) while taking belimumab, because this medicine weakens your immune system and live vaccines could cause infection. Ask your doctor which vaccines are safe for you. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially those with infections, since your immune system may not fight infections as well. Tell your doctor right away if you develop signs of infection such as fever, chills, cough, or painful urination. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy after your infusion or injection.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: serious allergic reaction symptoms such as hives, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing, or a sudden drop in blood pressure during or after your infusion or injection; signs of serious infection such as high fever, chills, severe cough, painful urination, or wounds that will not heal; new or worsening mental health symptoms such as depression, thoughts of suicide, or unusual changes in mood or behavior; signs of a blood clot such as sudden leg pain, swelling, or shortness of breath; new or unusual headaches or vision changes (which could be signs of a serious brain infection called PML, though rare). Also contact your doctor if you notice your lupus symptoms getting worse, if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, or if you have any questions or concerns about your treatment.
when_it_works: Belimumab works slowly over time. Most people do not feel results right away. It may take several months — often 6 months or longer — before you notice a clear improvement in your lupus symptoms or fewer flares. It is very important to keep taking your medicine even if you do not feel different at first. Do not stop taking belimumab without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Belimumab can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 4 months after your last dose. If you become pregnant, call your doctor right away. Breastfeeding: It is not known if belimumab passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Belimumab is approved for children 5 years and older with lupus. The dose is based on the child's weight and given as an IV infusion. Older adults: Belimumab can be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you carefully. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect your treatment plan. Always tell all of your healthcare providers that you are taking belimumab before starting any new medicines, vaccines, or treatments.
